tracks.name: Design Verification
tracks.blurb: SystemVerilog for testbenches, constrained random, coverage, assertions, UVM, and the whiteboard design questions DV loops ask.

items.title: Shallow copy, shared header
items.why: Copy semantics decide whether your scoreboard compares the transaction you meant or one the monitor already overwrote. This checks that you think in handles, not values.

prompt.x: What does this print?

items.question: What does the {{$display}} print?

options.why: That's what a deep copy would give. {{new p1}} copies the {{hdr}} handle, not the Header object it points to.
{{len}} is a plain int, so {{p2}} gets its own copy. Writing {{p2.len}} leaves {{p1.len}} at 4.
Backwards on both fields. Ints copy by value; class handles copy the reference.

hints: {{new p1}} makes a new Packet and copies each property into it. When the property is a class handle, what gets copied?
Draw the objects. After the copy, how many Packet objects exist, and how many Header objects?

solution.x: **Answer: 4 9.**

{{p2 = new p1;}} is a **shallow copy**. SystemVerilog allocates a new Packet and copies every property of {{p1}} into it. {{len}} is an int, so it's copied by value. {{hdr}} is a class handle, so the copy points at the same Header object as {{p1.hdr}}.
After the copy there are two Packets but only one Header. {{p2.len = 8}} changes only p2. {{p2.hdr.id = 9}} changes the shared Header, which p1 sees too.
A deep copy has to create the nested object as well:
In UVM you'd implement {{do_copy()}} and call {{clone()}} or {{copy()}} rather than writing this by hand.

followups.q: What prints if the copy line is {{p2 = p1;}} instead?
followups.a: {{8 9}}. That's a handle assignment, not a copy: no new object is created, so p1 and p2 are the same Packet.

followups.q: Why does this matter for a monitor?
followups.a: If a monitor reuses one transaction object and writes the same handle to its analysis port every time, every entry your scoreboard stored points at that one object, and they all change on the next sample. Create a new transaction (or clone it) before each write.

followups.q: Does {{new p1}} run Packet's constructor?
followups.a: No. The shallow copy allocates the object and copies the properties directly, so any setup code in {{new()}} is skipped.

items.title: Virtual or not
items.why: Polymorphism is how UVM swaps in a different driver or sequence without touching the env. If you can't predict which method body runs, factory overrides and callbacks will surprise you.
items.question: What does this print?

options.text: Child::show, then Child::name
options.why: {{show()}} isn't virtual in Base, so the call is bound by the handle's type (Base), not by the object's type.

options.text: Base::show, then Child::name
Base::show, then Base::name
options.why: {{name()}} is virtual in Base, so the object's real type (Child) picks the body, even through a Base handle.

options.text: Compile error: Child::name must be declared virtual
options.why: Once a method is virtual in the base class, overrides are virtual automatically. Repeating the keyword is optional.

hints: Two different rules are in play. One method is virtual and one isn't.
For a non-virtual method, the compiler decides using the handle's declared type. For a virtual method, the decision waits until run time.

solution.x: **Answer: Base::show, then Child::name.**

x: {{b.show()}}: {{show}} is not virtual, so the call is resolved at compile time from the handle type. {{b}} is a {{Base}} handle, so {{Base::show}} runs.

{{b.name()}}: {{name}} is virtual in Base, so the call is resolved at run time from the object type. The object is a {{Child}}, so {{Child::name}} runs. Child's override is virtual even without the keyword.

solution.x: Rule of thumb: declare any method you expect a subclass to override as {{virtual}} in the base class. UVM's phase methods, {{do_copy}}, {{do_compare}} and friends are all virtual for exactly this reason.

followups.q: Can you assign a Base handle to a Child handle?
followups.a: Not directly: {{c = b;}} is a compile error. Use {{$cast(c, b)}}, which succeeds only if {{b}} really points at a Child (or a subclass of Child).

followups.q: What's a pure virtual method?
followups.a: A method declared with no body, like {{pure virtual function void f();}}, inside a {{virtual class}}. Every non-abstract subclass must implement it, and the abstract class itself can't be constructed.

followups.q: What does {{super.name()}} do inside {{Child::name}}?
followups.a: It calls Base's implementation directly, skipping virtual dispatch. That's how an override extends the parent's behavior instead of replacing it.

items.title: Abstract classes and pure virtual methods
fork…join_any
items.why: Timeouts, watchdogs and parallel stimulus all use fork/join. Leaving threads alive by accident is a classic source of hangs and phantom errors at the end of a test.

prompt.x:
module tb;
  initial begin
    fork
      begin #10 $display("[%0t] A", $time); end
      begin #5  $display("[%0t] B", $time); end
      begin #20 $display("[%0t] C", $time); end
    join_any
    $display("[%0t] after fork", $time);
    #10 $display("[%0t] done", $time);
  end
endmodule

items.question: When does {{done}} print, and does {{C}} ever print?

options.text: done at 15; C still prints at 20
done at 15; C is killed and never prints
options.why: {{join_any}} only stops waiting. It doesn't kill the other threads; you need {{disable fork}} for that.

options.text: done at 30; C prints at 20
options.why: That's {{join}}, which waits for all threads. {{join_any}} resumes as soon as the first thread (B) finishes at time 5.

options.text: done at 20; C prints at 20
options.why: The parent resumes when B finishes at 5, then waits 10 more.

hints: Which thread finishes first, and at what time?
Does join_any do anything to the threads that are still running?

solution.x: **Answer: done at 15, and C still prints at 20.**

[5] B
[5] after fork
[10] A
[15] done
[20] C

{{join_any}} unblocks the parent when the **first** child finishes. B finishes at 5, so {{after fork}} prints at 5 and {{done}} at 15. A and C keep running in the background, and C prints at 20 even though the parent's code has finished.

x: {{join}}: wait for all children.
{{join_any}}: wait for the first child; the rest keep running.
{{join_none}}: don't wait at all; the children start when the parent next blocks.

followups.q: How do you kill the leftover threads?
followups.a: Call {{disable fork;}} after the join_any. It kills every child process of the current thread, not just this fork's, so wrap the whole thing in {{fork begin ... end join}} when you need to isolate it.

followups.q: Write the classic timeout pattern.
followups.a: Race the real work against a delay, then kill whichever one lost:

followups.q: What does {{wait fork;}} do?
followups.a: It blocks until all child processes of the current thread have finished. It's usually paired with {{join_none}}: spawn several threads, do other work, then wait for all of them.

items.title: disable fork and the timeout pattern
The solve…before trap
items.why: Constraints change distributions in ways people don't expect. A constraint like this one can quietly make writes rare, which shows up weeks later as a coverage hole.

prompt.x: There are no other constraints. You call {{t.randomize()}} many times.

items.question: What's the probability that {{is_write}} is 1?

options.why: That's what you'd get with {{solve is_write before burst}}. Without it, the solver picks uniformly over legal (is_write, burst) pairs, not one variable at a time.
Count the legal combinations: is_write = 0 allows 4 burst values, and is_write = 1 allows only 1.
That's the probability that is_write is 0.

hints: The solver picks uniformly among all legal combinations of the random variables.
List every (is_write, burst) pair that satisfies the constraint.

solution.x: **Answer: 1/5.**
Without {{dist}} or {{solve...before}}, the constraint solver picks uniformly among **all legal combinations** of the random variables. List them:

is_write  burst
   0        0
   0        1
   0        2
   0        3
   1        0      <- the only legal combination with is_write = 1
Five legal combinations, one with is_write = 1, so P = 1/5.

Adding {{solve is_write before burst;}} makes the solver pick {{is_write}} first (50/50), then pick {{burst}} from what's left. That gives P(is_write = 1) = 1/2. **solve...before changes the distribution, never which solutions are legal.**

followups.q: Without solve...before, what's P(burst == 0)?
followups.a: 2/5. Two of the five legal combinations have burst = 0: (0, 0) and (1, 0).

followups.q: With {{solve is_write before burst}}, what's P(burst == 0)?
followups.a: 5/8. is_write = 1 (probability 1/2) forces burst = 0. is_write = 0 (probability 1/2) gives burst = 0 one time in four. 1/2 + 1/8 = 5/8.

followups.q: Can you use solve...before on a randc variable?
followups.a: No. randc variables aren't allowed in solve...before; the solver always handles them before rand variables.

items.title: Constraining the sum of an array
Counting cross bins
items.why: Coverage numbers are only meaningful if you know what the bins are. Interviewers check that you can read a covergroup and predict how big the coverage space is.
items.question: How many bins does the cross {{x_addr_op}} have?

traps.msg: You counted cp_addr as 3 bins. {{mid[]}} makes one bin per value, and {{high[2]}} splits its range into 2 bins.
Close. {{high[2]}} splits [8:15] into two bins, [8:11] and [12:15].
Close. {{mid[]}} creates a separate bin for each value 4, 5, 6 and 7.
Only values named in bins count. cp_addr has 7 bins, not 16.
That's cp_addr alone. A cross has one bin per combination of its coverpoints' bins.

hints: Count cp_addr's bins first. {{low}}, {{mid[]}} and {{high[2]}} each create a different number of bins.
A coverpoint on an enum with no bins listed gets one automatic bin per enum value. The cross is the product.

solution.x: **Answer: 21.**

x: {{bins low = {[0:3]};}}: one bin covering 0 to 3. **1 bin.**
{{bins mid[] = {[4:7]};}}: empty brackets mean one bin per value. **4 bins.**
{{bins high[2] = {[8:15]};}}: split the range evenly into 2 bins, [8:11] and [12:15]. **2 bins.**
cp_addr total: 1 + 4 + 2 = **7**.
{{cp_op}} has no bins listed, so it gets one automatic bin per enum value: **3**.
The cross has one bin per combination: 7 × 3 = **21**.

followups.q: How would you remove IDLE from the cross?
followups.a: Add ignore_bins to the cross. That leaves 7 × 2 = 14 bins.

followups.q: ignore_bins vs illegal_bins?
followups.a: Both remove values from the coverage count. illegal_bins also raises an error if one of those values is ever sampled, so use it for values the design must never produce.

followups.q: Coverage is 100% but you're not done. How?
followups.a: Coverage only measures the bins you wrote. If the covergroup misses a feature, a corner case (back-to-back operations, reset mid-transaction), or samples at the wrong time, 100% means nothing. Review covergroups against the spec, not against the RTL.

items.title: Write a coverage plan for a FIFO
Where does it fail?
items.why: Reading an assertion against a waveform is daily DV work, and it's the fastest way for an interviewer to see whether you really understand implication and delay ranges.

prompt.x: Values are sampled at each rising edge of {{clk}}. The numbers above the waveform are cycles.

items.question: At which cycle does the assertion report a failure?

options.text: It never fails
options.why: Look at the request in cycle 5. gnt is low in cycles 6 and 7.

options.text: Cycle 5
options.why: The attempt that starts in cycle 5 can still pass until its window closes. Nothing has failed yet in cycle 5.

options.text: Cycle 7
Cycle 8
options.why: gnt in cycle 8 is one cycle too late, and the failure is reported as soon as the window closes in cycle 7.

hints: An attempt only matters when req is 1. In which cycles is req high?
{{|->}} starts checking the consequent in the same cycle req is seen. {{##[1:2]}} then allows gnt 1 or 2 cycles later. When does the second window run out?

solution.x: **Answer: cycle 7.**
An attempt starts at every clock edge. When {{req}} is 0 the implication passes **vacuously**, so only cycles 2 and 5 matter.

x: **Attempt from cycle 2.** {{|->}} is overlapping, so the consequent starts in cycle 2, and {{##[1:2] gnt}} looks for gnt in cycle 3 or 4. gnt is 1 in cycle 3: **pass at cycle 3**.
**Attempt from cycle 5.** The window is cycles 6 and 7. gnt is 0 in both, so the attempt **fails at cycle 7**, when the last chance runs out. The gnt in cycle 8 is too late to count.

solution.x: The waveform now shows both results.

followups.q: Write the same check with {{|=>}}.
followups.a: {{req |=> ##[0:1] gnt}}. Non-overlapping implication starts the consequent one cycle after req, so the delay range shifts down by one.

followups.q: What's a vacuous success, and why worry about it?
followups.a: When the antecedent (req) is false, the implication passes trivially. An assertion that only ever passes vacuously proves nothing, so pair it with a cover property such as {{cover property (@(posedge clk) req ##[1:2] gnt);}} to show the real case happened.

followups.q: How do you stop it firing during reset?
followups.a: Add {{disable iff (!rst_n)}} after the clocking event. It aborts any attempt in progress while rst_n is low.

items.title: UVM phase order
items.why: Almost every UVM bug that shows up as a null handle or a test that ends at time 0 comes back to phasing. It's one of the first UVM questions in DV screens.

prompt.x: Consider three UVM phases: {{build_phase}}, {{connect_phase}} and {{run_phase}}.

items.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: build_phase runs bottom-up, so child components exist before their parents.
options.why: It's top-down. A parent's build_phase is what creates its children.

options.text: build_phase runs top-down, connect_phase runs bottom-up, and of the three, only run_phase consumes simulation time.
All three are tasks, so you can put #delays in any of them.
options.why: build_phase and connect_phase are functions and must finish in zero time. Only run_phase (and the run-time sub-phases) are tasks.

options.text: Each component's run_phase starts after its parent's run_phase finishes.
options.why: Every component's run_phase starts at the same time and runs in parallel.

hints: Who creates a child component? Its parent, inside one of these phases.
Which of these is declared as a {{task}} rather than a {{function}}?

solution.x: **Answer: build top-down, connect bottom-up, and only run_phase consumes time.**

build_phase               function   top-down    create children, read config
connect_phase             function   bottom-up   connect TLM ports
end_of_elaboration_phase  function   bottom-up   final topology checks
start_of_simulation_phase function   bottom-up   print banners, set verbosity
run_phase                 task       parallel    drive and monitor stimulus
extract / check / report  function   bottom-up   collect and judge results
final_phase               function   top-down    close files

build_phase is top-down because a parent has to exist, and configure its children through {{uvm_config_db}}, before it creates them. run_phase is the only one of the three declared as a {{task}}; it ends when every raised objection has been dropped.

followups.q: What happens if nobody raises an objection in run_phase?
followups.a: The run phase ends right away, at time 0, and the test finishes without driving anything. Raise an objection in your test (or sequence) and drop it when the stimulus is done.

followups.q: run_phase vs main_phase?
followups.a: run_phase is one task that spans the whole simulation. main_phase is one of the run-time sub-phases (reset, configure, main, shutdown) that run in parallel with it and let components synchronize on stages. Many teams use only run_phase.

followups.q: Where do you get a virtual interface handle?
followups.a: In build_phase, with {{uvm_config_db#(virtual my_if)::get(this, "", "vif", vif)}}, after the top module sets it before {{run_test()}}. Fail with {{`uvm_fatal}} if the get returns 0.

items.title: Why type_id::create?
items.why: The factory is how one test injects errors or a different driver without editing the environment. Bypassing it is an easy bug that compiles cleanly, so interviewers like it.

prompt.x: {{err_driver}} extends {{base_driver}}, and both are registered with {{`uvm_component_utils}}.

items.question: What does the agent end up with?

options.text: An err_driver, because the override applies to every base_driver.
options.why: Overrides live in the factory, and {{new()}} never asks the factory.

options.text: A base_driver. Calling new() directly bypasses the factory, so the override never applies.
A compile error, because overrides require type_id::create.
options.why: It compiles fine. Nothing forces you to use the factory, which is why this bug is so easy to ship.

options.text: A runtime fatal, because the override target isn't registered.
options.why: Both classes are registered. The problem is how the driver is created.

hints: Where are overrides stored, and who checks them?
Does {{new()}} ever consult the factory?

solution.x: **Answer: a base_driver.**

An override is an entry in the UVM factory: "whenever someone asks for a base_driver, build an err_driver instead". The factory only gets a say when you create the object through it. {{new()}} is plain SystemVerilog construction, so the override is never checked.

// in the agent's build_phase
drv = base_driver::type_id::create("drv", this);

With {{type_id::create}}, the factory looks up overrides at creation time and returns an err_driver. That's why every component and transaction in a reusable env should be created through the factory.

followups.q: Why does the test set the override before {{super.build_phase()}}?
followups.a: The env and agent are created inside super.build_phase(). An override registered after they're built only affects objects created later.

followups.q: Type override vs instance override?
followups.a: A type override replaces every factory creation of that type. An instance override ({{set_inst_override_by_type}}) replaces it only at matching hierarchical paths, such as one agent out of four.

followups.q: Does the factory work for transactions too?
followups.a: Yes. Register them with {{`uvm_object_utils}}, create them with {{type_id::create}}, and a test can swap in a subclass with extra constraints, for example one that forces error responses.

items.title: TLM ports, exports and analysis ports
Reset in the middle of a test
Layered sequences for a protocol stack
Reusing a block env at subsystem level
Out-of-order scoreboard
items.why: "Design a scoreboard" is one of the most common DV whiteboard questions. It tests whether you think about every way a DUT can be wrong, not just mismatched data.

prompt.x: A DUT accepts read requests tagged with a 4-bit ID and returns responses **in any order**. At most one request per ID is outstanding at a time.
Design the scoreboard. Decide what data structure holds expected responses, how you match a response to its request, and what you check when the test ends.
Sketch it on paper or in EDA Playground, then check your design against the list below before opening the reference.

items.question: Check your design against each point:
rubric: Expected responses are keyed by ID (an associative array or array of queues), not kept in a single in-order FIFO.
A response whose ID has nothing outstanding is flagged as an error.
A response that doesn't match its prediction is flagged.
A new request that reuses an ID still outstanding is flagged.
At end of test, anything still outstanding is reported as a lost response.
Expected values come from a reference model, never copied from the DUT's own outputs.
hints: A FIFO assumes responses come back in request order. What structure lets you look up an entry by ID in one step?
List every way the DUT could misbehave: wrong data, a response nobody asked for, a response that never comes, a reused ID.

solution.x: **Reference design.** Keep expected responses in an associative array keyed by ID. Requests insert, responses look up, compare and delete, and check_phase reports anything left behind.
{{predict()}} stands in for your reference model. The two {{`uvm_analysis_imp_decl}} macros let one component receive from two monitors, with calls routed to {{write_req}} and {{write_rsp}}.
Why not a FIFO: an in-order queue reports a false mismatch the first time the DUT legally reorders two responses. The associative array makes order irrelevant and the lookup constant-time.

followups.q: What if the same ID can be outstanding more than once?
followups.a: Then ID alone isn't a key. If the spec guarantees responses for one ID come back in order, use an associative array of queues ({{txn expected[bit [3:0]][$];}}). Otherwise match on ID plus something else, like the address. Ask the interviewer what ordering the spec guarantees.

followups.q: How do you catch a response that never arrives before the test ends?
followups.a: Timestamp each entry on insert and run a watchdog in run_phase that flags any entry older than the spec's maximum latency.

followups.q: Where should predict() live?
followups.a: In a separate predictor or reference-model component that subscribes to the request monitor, so the scoreboard only compares. The model stays reusable and is easier to debug on its own.

tracks.name: RTL Design
tracks.blurb: Synthesizable SystemVerilog, FSMs, FIFOs, clock-domain crossing and timing: the fundamentals behind design and DV screens alike.

items.title: Spot the latch
items.why: Unintended latches are the most common RTL bug in new-grad code. Interviewers want to see that you read a combinational block and immediately ask: is every output assigned on every path?

prompt.x: Each block is meant to be combinational. {{y}}, {{d}}, {{a}}, {{b}}, {{c}} and {{en}} are 1-bit logic; {{sel}} is 2 bits.

items.question: Which one infers a latch?

options.text: Default first, then if
options.why: The default assignment at the top means y gets a value on every path.

options.text: if with no else
case with default
options.why: The default branch covers every sel value not listed, so y is always assigned.

options.text: Ternary assign
options.why: A continuous assignment with both branches of the ternary is pure combinational logic.

hints: For each block, ask what y should be when en is 0 (or when sel is 2'b11).
If the code doesn't say, the hardware has to remember the old value. What remembers a value without a clock edge?

solution.x: **Answer: the if with no else.**

When {{en}} is 0, nothing assigns {{y}}, so it must keep its previous value. Holding a value while an enable is low is exactly what a level-sensitive latch does, so synthesis infers one. With {{always_comb}}, most tools also warn that the block isn't purely combinational.
Three standard fixes, each giving y a value on every path:

always_comb begin
  y = 1'b0;            // 1. default assignment first
  if (en) y = d;
end

always_comb begin
  if (en) y = d;
  else    y = 1'b0;    // 2. complete if/else
end

assign y = en ? d : 1'b0;   // 3. continuous assignment

followups.q: Why are unintended latches a problem?
followups.a: They're transparent while enabled, so glitches pass straight through; they complicate static timing analysis and test insertion; and they almost always mean the RTL doesn't do what the designer intended.

followups.q: When is a latch intentional?
followups.a: Integrated clock-gating cells use a latch to hold the enable stable while the clock is high, and some high-performance designs use latch-based pipelines to borrow time between stages. Write intentional latches with {{always_latch}} so the intent is explicit.

followups.q: Does a missing else in {{always_ff}} infer a latch?
followups.a: No. In clocked logic, holding the old value is what a flip-flop already does, so you get a flop with an enable, not a latch.

items.title: The shift register that isn't
items.why: Blocking vs nonblocking assignment is the first thing an RTL interviewer probes. The bug here compiles, simulates and synthesizes without errors, and gives you the wrong hardware.

prompt.x: This was meant to be a 3-stage shift register.

items.question: How many rising clock edges after {{d}} changes does {{q}} show the new value?

traps.msg: That's the intent. With blocking assignments, r1, r2 and q all take the new d at the same clock edge.
Each blocking assignment completes before the next line runs, so r2 reads the r1 value just written, and q reads the new r2.
q is assigned inside a clocked block, so it only changes at a clock edge.

hints: A blocking assignment {{=}} updates the variable immediately, before the next statement executes.
At one clock edge, trace the three statements in order. What value does {{r2 = r1}} read?

solution.x: **Answer: 1 edge.**

Blocking assignments execute in order and take effect immediately. At a clock edge, {{r1 = d}} updates r1, then {{r2 = r1}} reads the **new** r1 (which is d), then {{q = r2}} reads the new r2. All three registers get d at the same edge, so q follows d after one edge. Synthesis sees that nothing ever uses the old values of r1 and r2 and keeps a single flip-flop for q.
The fix is nonblocking assignments. Every right-hand side is sampled first, and all updates happen together at the end of the time step:

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  r1 <= d;
  r2 <= r1;     // old r1
  q  <= r2;     // old r2
end
Rule: nonblocking ({{<=}}) in sequential logic, blocking ({{=}}) in combinational logic.

followups.q: Would reversing the order of the blocking statements fix it?
followups.a: Technically yes: {{q = r2; r2 = r1; r1 = d;}} reads each register before overwriting it, so you get three stages. It works, but it's fragile. With nonblocking assignments the order stops mattering.

followups.q: Why use blocking assignments in always_comb?
followups.a: Combinational logic should see updated values immediately, like intermediate wires. Nonblocking assignments there can leave stale values for a delta cycle and cause simulation and synthesis to disagree.

followups.q: Would lint catch the original?
followups.a: Yes. Verilator's BLKSEQ warning and most commercial lint rule decks flag blocking assignments inside a clocked block.

items.title: Mux, decoder and encoder from scratch
Overlapping 1011 detector
items.why: Sequence detectors are the classic FSM whiteboard question. The overlap case separates people who memorized a state diagram from people who can build one.

prompt.x: Design a **Moore** FSM with a serial input {{x}} and an output {{found}} that goes high for one cycle each time the last four bits seen were {{1011}}. Overlapping matches count: the input {{1011011}} produces two detections.

items.question: What's the minimum number of states?

traps.msg: 4 is the Mealy count. A Moore machine needs one more state whose only job is to hold found high.
That's a 3-bit history register. Many of those histories behave identically; merge them by asking how much of 1011 each one has matched.
That's a 4-bit history register. Track only the longest prefix of 1011 you've matched so far.

hints: Name each state after how much of {{1011}} you've matched so far: nothing, 1, 10, 101, 1011.
From the matched state, the last bits seen are 1011. On the next bit, what's the longest prefix of 1011 that's also a suffix of what you've seen?

solution.x: **Answer: 5 states.** Name each state by the longest prefix of 1011 matched so far:

state   matched   x=0     x=1     found
S0      (none)    S0      S1      0
S1      1         S10     S1      0
S10     10        S0      S101    0
S101    101       S10     S1011   0
S1011   1011      S10     S1      1

The overlap lives in two transitions. From S1011 on a 0, the last bits are {{10110}}, whose longest useful suffix is {{10}}, so go to S10. On a 1 it's {{10111}}, suffix {{1}}, so go to S1. Also note S101 on a 0 goes to S10, not S0: {{1010}} still ends in {{10}}.

followups.q: How many states for a Mealy version?
followups.a: 4 (S0, S1, S10, S101). The output is asserted on the transition from S101 when x = 1, so no state is needed for "just matched". The Mealy output depends on x combinationally and appears one cycle earlier than the Moore output.

followups.q: What changes for non-overlapping detection?
followups.a: Only the transitions out of the matched state: after a detection, start fresh, so S1011 goes to S0 on a 0 and S1 on a 1. Still 5 states.

followups.q: Why {{unique case}}?
followups.a: It tells synthesis the items are mutually exclusive, and makes simulation warn if no item matches, for example if the state goes to X. Don't use it to paper over incomplete decoding.

items.title: Full or empty?
items.why: Every DV and design loop gets to FIFOs eventually. The extra pointer bit is the detail that shows you've actually built one.

prompt.x: A synchronous FIFO has 8 entries. Its read and write pointers are 4 bits wide: the low 3 bits address the RAM, and the extra MSB is used to tell full from empty. Both pointers start at 0 and increment by 1 per operation, wrapping from 15 to 0.

items.question: Which condition means the FIFO is full?

options.text: Pointers equal
options.why: That's empty: the writer is exactly where the reader is, with no lap between them.

options.text: Low bits equal, MSBs differ
Writer one ahead
options.why: That means exactly one entry is stored.

options.text: Writer MSB set
options.why: The MSB alone tells you which lap the writer is on, not how far it is ahead of the reader.

hints: The number of entries stored is {{wr_ptr - rd_ptr}}, modulo 16. What value does that take when the FIFO is full?
From reset, write 8 times without reading. What are the two pointers?

solution.x: **Answer: low bits equal and MSBs different.**

The occupancy is {{wr_ptr - rd_ptr}} (mod 16) and ranges from 0 to 8. After 8 writes from reset, {{wr_ptr = 4'b1000}} and {{rd_ptr = 4'b0000}}: same RAM address, but the writer is one full lap ahead. That's full. Same address and same MSB means no lap: empty.

followups.q: Why not use plain 3-bit pointers?
followups.a: With 3 bits, the pointers are equal both when the FIFO is empty and when it's full. Without the extra bit (or a separate count or flag), you can't tell the two apart.

followups.q: How does the full check change for an async FIFO with Gray-coded pointers?
followups.a: Compare the write pointer with the synchronized read pointer with its top two bits inverted. In Gray code, "MSBs differ, rest equal" becomes "top two bits differ, rest equal".

followups.q: What about an occupancy counter instead?
followups.a: Increment on write, decrement on read, hold on both. It's simple and gives almost-full thresholds for free, but it adds an adder to the timing path and doesn't work across clock domains.

items.title: How deep is the FIFO?
items.why: FIFO sizing comes up in design and DV interviews alike, and it's easy to get wrong by forgetting that the reader drains the FIFO while the burst arrives.

prompt.x: A producer writes bursts of **80 words** at **100 MHz**, one word per clock, with long idle gaps between bursts. The consumer reads one word per clock at **50 MHz**.
Assume reads start the moment a burst starts, and ignore synchronizer latency.

items.question: What's the minimum FIFO depth, in words, so no data is lost?

traps.msg: That's the whole burst. The reader drains the FIFO while the burst is still arriving.
Check the read rate: 50 MHz is one read every 20 ns, so 40 reads happen during the 800 ns burst.
That's how many words the reader takes in 400 ns. The burst lasts 80 × 10 ns = 800 ns.

hints: How long does the burst take to arrive?
How many words does the reader remove in that time? Whatever's left has to sit in the FIFO.

solution.x: **Answer: 40 words.**

x: Burst duration: 80 words × 10 ns = **800 ns**.
Words read during the burst: 800 ns ÷ 20 ns = **40**.
Words that must be stored: 80 − 40 = **40**.

solution.x: In general, depth = B × (1 − r_read / r_write), where r is the effective word rate on each side. Real designs add a few entries for synchronizer latency and clock phase, and async FIFOs usually round up to a power of two.

followups.q: What if the reader only reads every other cycle?
followups.a: Its effective rate halves to 25 M words/s, so 20 words are read during the burst and depth = 80 − 20 = 60.

followups.q: How long must the gap between bursts be?
followups.a: Long enough to drain what's left: 40 words at one per 20 ns is 800 ns. With shorter gaps, the FIFO starts the next burst partly full and overflows.

followups.q: Why do async FIFOs usually have power-of-two depths?
followups.a: Gray-coded pointers change only one bit per step, including the wrap from the last value back to 0, only when the pointer range is a power of two. Other depths need special encodings.

items.title: Binary to Gray
items.why: Gray code is the backbone of clock-domain crossing for counters and FIFO pointers. Interviewers expect the conversion to be instant.

prompt.x: Convert the 4-bit binary value {{4'b1011}} to Gray code.

items.question: Enter the 4 Gray code bits, MSB first:

traps.msg: That's the conversion in the other direction (Gray to binary). Binary to Gray is {{g = b ^ (b >> 1)}}.
That's the input unchanged. Each Gray bit is the XOR of two neighboring binary bits.
Shift right, not left: {{g = b ^ (b >> 1)}}, and the MSB passes through unchanged.

hints: The Gray MSB equals the binary MSB.
Every other Gray bit is the XOR of that binary bit and the bit just above it: {{g[i] = b[i+1] ^ b[i]}}.

followups.q: Convert Gray 1110 back to binary.
followups.a: b3 = 1, b2 = 1 ^ 1 = 0, b1 = 0 ^ 1 = 1, b0 = 1 ^ 0 = 1, giving 1011. You get back where you started.

followups.q: Why does Gray code help with clock-domain crossing?
followups.a: Adjacent values differ in exactly one bit. If the receiving domain samples mid-change, only that one bit can be uncertain, so it settles to either the old or the new value, never a value that was never there.

followups.q: Does Gray code help if the counter jumps by 2?
followups.a: No. The single-bit-change property only holds between consecutive values. A pointer that can skip values has to be moved some other way, like a handshake.

items.title: Moving a counter across clock domains
items.why: CDC bugs survive simulation and show up in silicon. Interviewers want to hear why a multi-bit bus can't just go through per-bit synchronizers.

prompt.x: A 4-bit counter in a **200 MHz** domain increments by 1 on enabled cycles. Logic in an **unrelated 75 MHz** domain needs to read its value.

items.question: Which approach gives the 75 MHz side a valid, if slightly stale, count?

options.text: Put a 2-flop synchronizer on each of the 4 binary bits.
options.why: Each bit's synchronizer can resolve on a different cycle. From 0111 to 1000, four bits change at once, and the receiver can briefly see values like 1111 or 0000.

options.text: Convert the count to Gray code in the 200 MHz domain, register it, then pass each bit through a 2-flop synchronizer.
Capture the bus with a single flop in the 75 MHz domain.
options.why: One flop leaves no time for metastability to resolve, and it doesn't fix the multi-bit problem either.

options.text: Sample the bus on the falling edge of the 75 MHz clock to avoid the setup window.
options.why: With unrelated clocks there's no safe edge. The source can change at any point relative to either edge.

hints: How many bits change when a binary counter goes from 7 to 8? What could the receiver see if each bit settles on a different cycle?
Which encoding changes exactly one bit per increment?

solution.x: **Answer: Gray-code the count, register it, then synchronize each bit.**

Per-bit synchronizers are safe for one bit. For a bus, each bit can resolve a cycle apart, so a binary count changing from {{0111}} to {{1000}} can be seen as a mix of old and new bits that was never a real value.

A Gray count changes exactly one bit per increment. If the receiver samples mid-change, only that bit is uncertain, and it resolves to either the old or the new value. Either way, the receiver sees a value the counter really held. Registering the Gray value in the source domain first matters too: it keeps glitches from the conversion logic out of the synchronizer.
This is exactly how async FIFO pointers cross domains. For arbitrary data (not a counter), use a handshake or an async FIFO.

followups.q: The source counts faster than the destination samples. Is that OK?
followups.a: Yes. The receiver may skip values (it sees 3, then 6), but every value it sees was real. For FIFO pointers, a stale pointer just makes full or empty slightly conservative.

followups.q: How do you move an arbitrary 32-bit value across?
followups.a: Hold the data stable, send a single request bit through a synchronizer, capture the data in the destination, and synchronize an acknowledge back. Use an async FIFO when you need throughput.

followups.q: What's synchronizer MTBF, and what improves it?
followups.a: Mean time between synchronizer failures. It grows exponentially with the time a flop gets to resolve, so adding a third flop, or lowering the destination clock rate, improves it dramatically.

items.title: Async FIFO pointers end to end
Maximum clock frequency
items.why: Setup and hold are the vocabulary of timing closure. Expect this as a warm-up in any design or physical design screen, often followed by a hold question.

prompt.x: A register-to-register path has clock-to-Q **0.20 ns**, worst-case combinational delay **3.50 ns**, and setup time **0.30 ns**. Assume no clock skew or jitter.

items.question: What's the maximum clock frequency, in MHz?

traps.msg: You left out setup time. Data has to arrive t_setup before the capturing edge.
Clock-to-Q and setup time are part of the cycle too, not just the logic delay.
4 ns is the minimum period. Convert: f = 1 / T.

hints: Data launches at one edge and must be captured at the next. What has to fit into one clock period?
T_min = t_clk-to-Q + t_comb + t_setup. Then f_max = 1 / T_min.

solution.x: **Answer: 250 MHz.**
T_min = t_cq + t_comb,max + t_setup = 0.20 + 3.50 + 0.30 = **4.00 ns**, so f_max = 1 / 4.00 ns = **250 MHz**.
With clock skew (capture clock arrival minus launch clock arrival):

setup:  T  >=  t_cq + t_comb,max + t_setup - t_skew
hold:   t_cq + t_comb,min  >=  t_hold + t_skew

followups.q: The capture clock arrives later than the launch clock (positive skew). Good or bad?
followups.a: It helps setup, because the cycle is effectively longer, and hurts hold, because new data can race through before the capturing flop's hold window closes.

followups.q: How do you fix a hold violation?
followups.a: Add delay to the short path, usually buffers the tools insert. Slowing the clock doesn't help, because the hold check doesn't depend on the clock period.

followups.q: How do you fix a setup violation?
followups.a: Shorten the path: simplify or restructure the logic, retime registers, split it into two pipeline stages, use faster cells, or relax the clock.

items.title: A wide RAM from narrow ones

tracks.name: Computer Architecture
tracks.blurb: Caches, virtual memory, pipelines, out-of-order execution and coherence: the conceptual core of CPU, GPU and SoC interviews.

items.title: Slice the address
items.why: Splitting an address into tag, index and offset is the foundation for every cache question that follows. Interviewers expect it in under a minute.

prompt.x: A **32 KiB**, **4-way set-associative** cache has **64-byte** lines. Addresses are 32-bit byte addresses.

items.question: How many tag bits does each line store?

traps.msg: That's a direct-mapped cache (512 sets). With 4 ways there are 128 sets, so 7 index bits.
Recheck the set count: 32 KiB / (64 B × 4 ways) = 128 sets, which is 7 index bits, not 6.
That's a fully associative cache, which has no index bits. This one has 128 sets.
Recheck the set count: 32 KiB / (64 B × 4 ways) = 128 sets, which is 7 index bits.

hints: Offset bits come from the line size. Index bits come from the number of sets.
Sets = capacity / (line size × ways). Tag = 32 − index − offset.

solution.x: **Answer: 19 bits.**

x: Offset: 64-byte lines need log2(64) = **6 bits**.

followups.q: How much tag storage in total?
followups.a: 512 lines × 19 bits = 9,728 bits, plus a valid bit per line (and a dirty bit if it's write-back).

followups.q: Make it 8-way at the same size. What changes?
followups.a: Sets halve to 64, the index drops to 6 bits, and the tag grows to 20 bits. Offset is unchanged.

followups.q: Can this cache be virtually indexed and physically tagged with 4 KiB pages?
followups.a: Not without extra care. Index plus offset is 13 bits, but a 4 KiB page leaves only 12 bits untranslated, so one physical line could land in two different sets (aliasing). That's one reason many 32 KiB L1 caches are 8-way: 4 KiB per way keeps index plus offset inside the page offset.

items.title: Count the misses
items.why: Walking an access trace by hand shows you understand mapping, eviction and miss types. It's a common whiteboard exercise that often leads into associativity trade-offs.

prompt.x: A **direct-mapped** cache has **4 lines** of **16 bytes** each and starts empty. The CPU reads these byte addresses in order:

items.question: How many of the 7 accesses miss?

traps.msg: 4 is the number of distinct blocks touched (compulsory misses). Some of those blocks also evict each other.
0x04 is in the same 16-byte block as 0x00, so it hits.
That's the answer for a 2-way cache. Check which set 0x00, 0x40, 0x80 and 0x44 map to here.

hints: Block number = address / 16. Set = block number mod 4.
Write down the block and set for every access. How many different blocks want set 0?

solution.x: **Answer: 6 misses.**

address  block  set  result
0x00       0     0   miss  (compulsory)
0x04       0     0   hit   (same block)
0x40       4     0   miss  (compulsory, evicts block 0)
0x00       0     0   miss  (conflict, evicts block 4)
0x80       8     0   miss  (compulsory, evicts block 0)
0x44       4     0   miss  (conflict, evicts block 8)
0x10       1     1   miss  (compulsory)
Blocks 0, 4 and 8 all map to set 0 and keep evicting each other, while sets 2 and 3 stay empty the whole time. That's a **conflict** problem, not a capacity problem.

followups.q: Same capacity, 2-way set-associative with LRU?
followups.a: 5 misses. Blocks 0, 4 and 8 still share a set, but with two ways the second access to 0x00 hits.

followups.q: Classify the 6 misses.
followups.a: Compulsory: the first touch of blocks 0, 4, 8 and 1 (4 misses). Conflict: the second 0x00 and 0x44 (2 misses). No capacity misses, since the cache is never full.

followups.q: Fully associative with LRU?
followups.a: 4 misses, all compulsory. Four distinct blocks fit in four lines.

items.title: AMAT with two levels
items.why: Average memory access time is how architects compare cache designs. Interviewers check that you apply each miss rate only to the accesses that reach that level.

prompt.x: L1 hit time **1 cycle**, L1 miss rate **5%**. L2 hit time **10 cycles**, L2 local miss rate **20%**. Main memory latency **100 cycles**.

items.question: What's the average memory access time, in cycles?

traps.msg: The 20% L2 miss rate only applies to the 5% of accesses that miss in L1.
You skipped L2. L1 misses go to L2 first, and only L2's misses go to memory.
Every L1 miss pays the L2 hit time (10 cycles) before anything else.
L2 misses still have to go to main memory.

hints: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. What's L1's miss penalty?
L1's miss penalty is L2's own AMAT: 10 + 0.2 × 100.

solution.x: **Answer: 2.5 cycles.**
Treat L2 as L1's miss penalty:

followups.q: What's the global L2 miss rate?
followups.a: 0.05 × 0.20 = 1% of all accesses go to main memory.

followups.q: Halve L1's miss rate, or halve memory latency: which helps more?
followups.a: Halving L1 misses: 1 + 0.025 × 30 = 1.75 cycles. Halving memory latency: 1 + 0.05 × (10 + 10) = 2.0 cycles. The L1 change wins here.

followups.q: Why not just make L1 bigger?
followups.a: Larger caches have longer hit times, and L1's hit time is paid on every access. So L1 stays small and fast, and extra capacity goes into L2 and L3.

items.title: Write-back, write-allocate
items.why: Write policies determine memory traffic and coherence behavior. Verification engineers on cache and memory teams have to know exactly what each policy does on a store miss.

prompt.x: A cache uses a **write-back, write-allocate** policy. A store misses in the cache.

items.question: What happens?

options.text: The store goes straight to memory, and the cache is unchanged.
options.why: That's no-write-allocate, usually paired with write-through.

options.text: The line is fetched into the cache, the store updates the cached copy and marks it dirty, and memory is updated only when the line is evicted.
The store updates both the cache and memory immediately.
options.why: That's write-through. Write-back defers the memory update until eviction.

options.text: The store is held in a buffer, and the line is invalidated in the cache.
options.why: Write buffers exist, but a store miss doesn't invalidate anything under this policy.

hints: Write-allocate answers: on a store miss, does the line come into the cache?
Write-back answers: when does memory see the new data?

solution.x: **Answer: fetch the line, write the cached copy, mark it dirty, write memory on eviction.**

on a store hit               on a store miss
write-back       update cache, set dirty      (depends on allocate policy)
write-through    update cache and memory      (depends on allocate policy)

write-allocate      store miss: fetch the line, then treat it as a hit
no-write-allocate   store miss: write memory only, don't fetch the line
Common pairings are write-back with write-allocate (most CPU caches) and write-through with no-write-allocate.

followups.q: Why pair write-back with write-allocate?
followups.a: If writes are going to live in the cache, bring the line in so later writes to it hit. Write-back without allocate would send every store miss to memory anyway.

followups.q: What does the dirty bit save?
followups.a: On eviction, clean lines are dropped with no memory write. Only dirty lines are written back.

followups.q: What's write-through's advantage?
followups.a: Memory always holds the latest data, which simplifies coherence and error recovery. A write buffer hides most of the extra store latency.

items.title: How big is the page table?
items.why: Virtual memory questions start here and move to TLBs and multi-level tables. Memory-management (MMU) verification teams ask this kind of question often.

prompt.x: A system uses **32-bit** virtual addresses, **4 KiB** pages, a **single-level** page table, and **4-byte** page table entries.

items.question: How big is one process's page table, in MiB?

traps.msg: Right size, wrong unit: 4096 KiB is 4 MiB.
That's the number of entries. Each entry is 4 bytes.
2^20 entries × 4 bytes is 4 MiB, not 1.

hints: How many bits of the address are the page offset? The rest is the virtual page number.
One entry per virtual page: 2^(VPN bits) entries × 4 bytes.

solution.x: **Answer: 4 MiB.**

x: Page offset: 4 KiB = 2^12, so **12 bits**.
Virtual page number: 32 − 12 = **20 bits**, so 2^20 = 1,048,576 entries.
Size: 2^20 × 4 bytes = 2^22 bytes = **4 MiB**, for every process, even one that uses almost no memory.

followups.q: Why do real systems use multi-level page tables?
followups.a: Most of a process's address space is unused. With a two-level 10/10 split, you always need the 4 KiB top level, but second-level tables only for regions actually in use, often a few dozen KiB instead of 4 MiB.

followups.q: What's the TLB reach of 64 entries with 4 KiB pages?
followups.a: 64 × 4 KiB = 256 KiB. Workloads that touch more than that miss in the TLB often, which is why huge pages (2 MiB) exist.

followups.q: How many memory accesses does a TLB miss cost with a 2-level table?
followups.a: Two page-table reads (one per level) before the actual data access, unless those entries are already cached.

items.title: The cost of a page walk
A page fault, end to end
The load-use stall
items.why: Pipeline hazards are the core of CPU core interviews. The load-use case is the one hazard forwarding can't fully hide, and interviewers like to see you draw the diagram.

prompt.x: A classic 5-stage in-order pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) has **full forwarding**. It runs:

lw   x1, 0(x2)
add  x3, x1, x4
sub  x5, x3, x6

items.question: How many stall cycles does this sequence incur?

traps.msg: Forwarding can't go back in time: lw has its data at the end of MEM, but add needs it at the start of EX in that same cycle.
The add → sub dependency is covered by EX → EX forwarding. Only the load-use pair stalls.
That's the answer without forwarding.

hints: Which pair of instructions has a dependency forwarding can fully cover, and which can't?
A load's data exists at the end of MEM. When does the next instruction need it?

solution.x: **Answer: 1 stall cycle.**

cycle   1    2    3    4    5    6    7    8
lw      IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
add          IF   ID   ID   EX   MEM  WB
sub               IF   IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB

lw's data is ready at the end of MEM (cycle 4). add needs it at the start of EX, so add's EX can't happen before cycle 5: it waits one cycle in ID, and sub waits behind it. From there, forwarding covers everything: MEM/WB → EX for x1 into add, and EX/MEM → EX for x3 into sub.

followups.q: How many stalls with no forwarding at all? (The register file writes in the first half of a cycle and reads in the second.)
followups.a: 4: two for lw → add and two more for add → sub, because each consumer's ID has to line up with its producer's WB.

followups.q: How can the compiler remove the stall?
followups.a: Schedule an independent instruction between the load and its first use, so the slot after the load does useful work.

followups.q: Which logic detects the stall?
followups.a: The hazard detection unit in ID. If the instruction in EX is a load whose destination matches a source register of the instruction in ID, it holds the PC and IF/ID register and inserts a bubble into EX.

items.title: What branches cost
items.why: CPI math connects microarchitecture to performance. Expect a branch-prediction question in nearly every CPU core loop.

prompt.x: A processor has a base CPI of **1.0**. **20%** of instructions are branches, the predictor is **90%** accurate, and a misprediction costs **3 cycles**.

items.question: What's the effective CPI?

traps.msg: That charges the penalty on every branch. Only the 10% that mispredict pay it.
You used the accuracy (90%) instead of the misprediction rate (10%).
You added the misprediction fraction (0.02) but forgot to multiply it by the 3-cycle penalty.

hints: What fraction of all instructions are mispredicted branches?
CPI = base + (mispredicts per instruction × penalty).

solution.x:
CPI = base + branch fraction × mispredict rate × penalty
    = 1.0 + 0.20 × 0.10 × 3
    = 1.06

followups.q: Same predictor on a deep pipeline with a 15-cycle penalty?
followups.a: 1 + 0.2 × 0.1 × 15 = 1.30. Deeper pipelines make predictor accuracy matter much more.

followups.q: Why does a 2-bit counter beat a 1-bit predictor on loops?
followups.a: A 1-bit predictor mispredicts twice per loop: at the exit, and again when the loop is next entered. A 2-bit saturating counter needs two wrong outcomes in a row to flip, so it only mispredicts the exit.

followups.q: Besides branches, what else stalls an in-order pipeline?
followups.a: Data hazards, like the load-use case, and structural hazards, where two instructions need the same resource in the same cycle.

items.title: The reorder buffer and precise exceptions
MESI on a read
items.why: Coherence protocols are where multicore bugs live, and coherence verification is a big part of CPU and SoC DV. Interviewers expect you to walk state transitions without notes.

prompt.x: Two cores use a snooping **MESI** protocol. Core A holds a line in **Modified**. Core B then reads that line and misses in its own cache.

items.question: What's the result?

options.text: A's copy stays M, and B gets the line in E.
options.why: E means "the only copy, and clean". Two caches can't both hold exclusive copies, and A's copy has to stop being the only one.

options.text: A supplies its dirty data (also writing it back to memory), and both copies end up in S.
A invalidates its copy, and B gets the line in M.
options.why: B only read. Invalidating other copies happens when B wants to write.

options.text: B's read waits until A evicts the line.
options.why: Snooping lets A respond right away. Waiting for an eviction could take forever.

hints: A has the only up-to-date copy. Memory's copy is stale.
After the read, how many caches hold the line, and are they allowed to write it without telling anyone?

solution.x: **Answer: A supplies the data and both end in S.**

M  Modified    only copy, dirty     may write silently
E  Exclusive   only copy, clean     may write silently (moves to M)
S  Shared      maybe other copies   must invalidate others before writing
I  Invalid     no valid copy

B's read miss goes on the bus. A snoops it, sees it holds the line in M, and flushes the dirty data so B (and memory) get the up-to-date copy. A drops to S, since it's no longer the only holder, and B loads the line in S.
MOESI adds an Owned state so A can keep the dirty data and keep supplying it, skipping the write to memory.

followups.q: Now B writes the line. What happens?
followups.a: B sends an invalidate (an upgrade request) on the bus. A's copy goes to I, and B's goes from S to M.

followups.q: What's the point of the E state?
followups.a: A core with a line in E can write it with no bus traffic, silently moving to M. Without E, the first write to private data would always broadcast an invalidate.

followups.q: What's false sharing?
followups.a: Two cores write different variables that happen to share a cache line. The line ping-pongs between their caches even though no data is actually shared. Fix it by padding or aligning the variables onto separate lines.
